transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-01
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Li (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (DataHarbor), Jordan Reed (DataHarbor SRE), Samir Khan (DataHarbor Platform), Emily Ortiz (DataHarbor Product)

Auto-generated Summary: went over harness integration and what DataHarbor needs to run realistic benchmarks. Lots of talk about streaming latencies and p95 targets, also about KV cache and prefix caching.

00:00 Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, yeah Alex from Redwood. quick round robin, who i think we've all met but welcome.
00:18 Maya Patel: Hey thanks, Maya here, head of ML at DataHarbor. we're really trying to validate cost + latency for a near-prod workload.
00:30 Priya Shah: Great. The goal for today is to map your scripts into our harness, understand traffic shape, and align on success criteria.
00:45 Jordan Reed: Our main constraints are 99th p95-ish latency under 500ms for non-streaming generation at peak, and <1% error rate. Also concerned about tail latencies when concurrency spikes.
01:05 Alex Morgan: Right, and also we should confirm whether you want streaming responses in the POC or purely non-streaming to simplify measurement.
01:20 Samir Khan: We have a mix. Product uses streaming in chat features, but many batch jobs call non-streaming. we can share both script types.
01:35 Daniel Li: Cool. For the harness we support both streaming and non-streaming runs; metrics differ — streaming needs token-level latency and first-byte times, non-streaming looks at total response time and tokens/sec.
01:55 Emily Ortiz: Quick question on scripts: our current harness is Python + locust for load, and some internal async node scripts; will that map easily?
02:10 Priya Shah: Yes, we typically ingest customer scripts as a thin wrapper. We prefer a canonical runner (we'll send the repo) and a small shim you drop in. The shim captures timestamps for first-byte and final-byte for streaming.
02:30 Maya Patel: There have been transcription issues before where KV cache was mis-recorded, we use KV cache heavily for chat — it's critical to capture warm vs cold cache runs.
02:45 Alex Morgan: Good call. We should plan cold-start runs and warm cache runs. We'll need representative prefix distributions and sequence lengths.
03:05 Jordan Reed: For concurrency, typical peak is 150 concurrent chat sessions; each session averages 2-3 parallel token streams. For batch, peak is ~40 concurrent non-streaming requests with 1.2k tokens per request median.
03:30 Daniel Li: Got it. For sizing the harness we will create separate scenarios: chat-streaming (150 conc), chat-non-streaming equivalent, and batch (40 conc). We'll also run a ramp and a sustained plateau to measure degradation.
03:50 Priya Shah: Success criteria — what are the absolute KPIs? We'll propose: p95 < 500ms non-streaming for median 1.2k token requests, first-token latency < 150ms for streaming for short messages, throughput > X tokens/sec matching your traffic — can you confirm X?
04:20 Maya Patel: We're aiming for sustained 30k tokens/sec across the pool during batch windows. For chat streaming, the important thing is first-byte < 200ms, and p95 of end-to-end shouldn't exceed 1s for longer responses.
04:40 Alex Morgan: We'll map that to GPU sizing and concurrency buckets; also discuss quantization profiles. Are you ok with us recommending an int8 quantized model variant for cost tests?
04:55 Samir Khan: Possibly, but we need to ensure quality doesn't regress. We'll run a small eval set. want to see rouge/semantic similarity delta < 1.5% ideally.
05:15 Daniel Li: We'll include accuracy checks in the harness; we can add eval prompts and compute embeddings similarity to your golden outputs.
05:35 Jordan Reed: Network: we plan to run in our VPC with peered test subnets. Any constraints for egress or IP allowlists?
05:50 Priya Shah: We'll need a temporary allowlist for Redwood test agents and a service account key. We'll share the IP ranges and CICD windows in the runbook.
06:05 Alex Morgan: Timing: propose initial integration this week, initial dry run next Monday, full load test next Wednesday. That matches previous next-steps.
06:20 Maya Patel: Sounds good. Questions about observability — we need token-level traces, per-route cost breakdown, and per-request metadata for debugging.
06:35 Daniel Li: The harness will emit per-request JSON logs with timestamps, model id, route, tokens_in/out, and GPU/memory counters where available. note: sometimes GPU memory counters are approximate depending on the backend.
06:55 Emily Ortiz: On the streaming side, how do you measure token-level latencies? we need to attribute where slowdowns happen (model vs network).
07:10 Priya Shah: We instrument first-byte, per-50-token buckets, and final-byte. We also capture server-side timestamps when available so you can separate network and server timing. there might be clock skew; we recommend NTP sync.
07:30 Jordan Reed: Good. About benchmarking harness: will you run load generators from Redwood or do we run locally in our cloud?
07:45 Alex Morgan: We offer both. For most accurate network conditions we ask customers to run load agents in their VPC; Redwood can run a coordinated agent to validate. For this POC we recommend DataHarbor run the load agent in their region and we run a control runner.
08:05 Maya Patel: We'll run it. We'll send a terraform module to spin up an autoscaling load generator pool.
08:20 Daniel Li: Perfect. We'll document the required IAM roles and required ports.
08:30 Priya Shah: Edge cases: long-context runs and KV cache eviction patterns. We'll schedule a separate deep dive if you want to test very long contexts beyond 32k tokens.
08:45 Samir Khan: Not in first POC, we can cover up to 16k for now.
08:55 Alex Morgan: On model variants: we'll provision a baseline open model (redwood-llamax-13b-ish) and a quantized variant; we'll also test a slightly larger model to see cost/latency tradeoffs.
09:15 Maya Patel: If you could include cost-per-1M tokens estimates per profile that would be helpful.
09:30 Daniel Li: We'll include a cost table. note: cost numbers for dedicated vs hosted differ; we'll call out both.
09:45 Emily Ortiz: How do we capture retries and backpressure behavior in the harness? sometimes our frontends retry aggressively which masks real latency.
10:00 Priya Shah: We'll add a jittered retry policy to the harness and also run a no-retry scenario. We recommend capturing retry counts and origin of retry in logs.
10:20 Jordan Reed: Security: we need to ensure audit logs and SSO integration for the control plane. Also SOC2 docs.
10:35 Alex Morgan: We'll attach our SOC2 and ISO certs. For SSO, we can add a temporary SAML connection or service-account-based access for the POC.
10:50 Maya Patel: Great. Any blockers on your side to get the scripts in place?
11:00 Daniel Li: We'll need the sample scripts, and a description of expected headers/metadata you pass. Also tokenization differences matter for tokens/sec. please provide tokenization counts.
11:20 Samir Khan: We'll include that.
11:30 Priya Shah: Alright, recap of success criteria we heard: p95 non-streaming <500ms for 1.2k token median; streaming first-byte <200ms; sustained batch throughput 30k tokens/sec; error rate <1%; semantic quality delta <1.5%.
11:55 Alex Morgan: Next steps: Alex to send runbook + repo, Priya to draft test plan and matrix, DataHarbor to send scripts and traces, schedule run next Wednesday.
12:10 Maya Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the traces link.
12:20 Alex Morgan: Thanks, talk soon.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and mis-typed acronyms (KV cache sometimes said as key-v cache), model names may be slightly off in the transcript. Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.company/bench-runbook (runbook), https://drive.company/s/dataharbor-traces (customer traces placeholder).
